#### 78.41 THE QUESTION SHEET: QUESTIONS IN A FIXED FIRST ORDER, DEPTH BY STAKE AND FACT (2026-11-12; Kaveh: "we're asking a bunch of questions. First set of questions is between us and the chess board ... The next set of questions includes the opponent response. The order of the questions is the most important thing, because it decides whether we have time to see the real threats/opportunities or not"; "we need to break them down logically"; "The order initially is my king first, then their king, then their queen, my queen, etc. But how deep on each question depends on the stakes and the facts ... Maybe we go a bit deep here, then a bit there, then if there's more time a bit deeper here")

A PROBE FIRST (scratch script, a general chess library and textbook unit worths, NOT engine code; the 4156 positions of 78.37's fresh games, seeds 11 12 13 at 0.2 s; a "bad move" is a MISSED surprise where the judge's reading fell):

READING: where a unit is in contact the short search already sees it and errs about half as often; where NO question says yes the mover errs most (the last line), and those positions hold four in ten of the bad moves; a confined king (either side's) is the one sign that raises the rate. The engine has no question for a quiet position and none for an attack that is not yet a contact.

DESIGN (generic: a TARGET is a unit, its STAKE comes from the goal clause for the goal unit and from the judge's worth for the rest; nothing names a game):
  QUESTION   one target and one side asking: "can this target be taken or confined, and by what". The first order is by stake, sides alternating: mine at the top stake, theirs at the top stake, theirs at the next, mine at the next, and so on down.
  BREAKDOWN  each question is a tree of smaller ones, and a NO closes everything under it.
             level 0, the board as it stands: where is the target, what strikes it now, what guards it, which of its exits are open (78.39's HOLES and COVERED).
             level 1, one side's moves alone: which units could come to strike or cover, in how many moves (78.39's SUPPLY and SCENARIOS). No supplier closes the question: the target is SAFE from that side, and the sheet says why.
             level 2 and on, with the other side's reply: can the plan be stopped (cover, exchange, a counter at a higher stake); an exact search over the moves the question names, one ply deeper each time it is asked again.
             the quiet question, when every question above is closed or idle: which unit of mine does least (fewest strikes, fewest places to go), and where would it do more.
  SCHEDULE   anytime. Every open question holds its stake, its level, what it has cost and what its last step found. The next step goes to the question with the most at stake per unit of cost among those still open; a step that finds nothing new lowers its question's urgency, a step that finds a live plan raises it. So the clock goes a little here, a little there, and deeper where the facts keep it open. The sheet's answer at any moment is the list of open questions with their best lines; the move search starts from those lines.
  MEASURES   (a) the share of bad-move positions in which no question is open should fall against the probe's last line; (b) the level-1 SAFE verdicts should be right (the judge agrees no loss follows); (c) cost per step, and the order of steps printed in plain words; (d) later, the surprise rate of 78.37 with the sheet's lines as the search's first moves.
  STAGE 1    the sheet and the schedule as a training-side tool over the existing engine calls (facts, 78.39's scenario for any target, the ledger search for the reply levels); measures (a) to (c). Not yet in the wake.

(2) WHAT THEY ARE: in seven of ten the judge preferred a quiet move to our quiet move, in one of ten a check; a missed capture is rare (1.4%). (3) THE DIFFERENCE THE SHEET DOES SEE IS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE BOARD: after the judge's move the stake of THEIR units live at level 0 is 5.26 against 2.06 after ours and 1.93 after a random other move; the questions on MY units read the same after both (0.72 and 0.85 live, 39.19 and 39.09 open). Our move keeps our units as safe as the judge's does and makes no more threats than a random move. The engine answers "is anything of mine about to be lost" and does not ask "what can I attack". (4) The search step is dear as built (89.20 ms a step at depth 2, 343.79 ms at depth 3) and leaves 4740 ways not settled because a quiet first move takes nothing and threatens nothing at once: its value is in the question it opens, which is the next thing to count.
OPEN: the value of a way is a formula over the reason chain's answers, not a full exchange; a quiet move's worth to a question is unread; the run with search takes 1720.7 s for 400 positions.

OCTOBER'S FRAMES LOOKED AT AGAIN (Kaveh: "check out the frame methods from october, we were pretty good at solving puzzles there"; a read of JOURNAL 2026-10-07 to 10-24 and the code): a frame was a small game with its own moves and EXITS, searched to its own size and not to a fixed ply (the exchange on one place, the forcing line, the cornered unit whose top case is the goal unit, the promotion, the double threat, and WAITING frames with what they wait on and what breaks them); questions by stake; a memory keyed by what each result read. Its proofs were right (67 of 69 at 15 s a puzzle) and its unproved picks were not (5 of 21); quiet moves 24 to 27 of 100; skipping the replies outside the frame was wrong in 10.9% and was switched off. Game-free and still in the tree: catspace/incubator/analyst/frame_search.py (the Frame protocol, exits, retractable records) and rust/analyst_core/src/agenda.rs; the frames themselves are bound to a chess library.

#### 78.42 THE QUESTION GRAPH: THE CHECKER IN TWO LAYERS, OBSTACLES BY COUNTERFACTUAL, STAKES AS BOUNDS, THE CLOCK BY EXPECTED STAKE (2026-11-13; Kaveh, in order: "the cheap check ... should basically say that to ... the one that's doing the slow calculation ... like a scout giving a location ... take a right and then take a left ... it should always go for the entire flow"; "the waiting frame needs to come in"; "go back to the October code and port over everything that is useful ... assume that it already exists"; "the fact that it's considering pieces as fixed is a big blind spot ... given the medium of movement and the rules of movement, how many hops is it going to take ... that's layer one of the checker. And then layer two of the checker would be the pieces ... the only way it wasn't here is either you capture it or it moves"; "I think of reasoning as a starting point and a chain of claims ... a graph structure ... every question inspires the next question"; "there's always going to be counterfactuals"; "there might be other obstacles, not just these three"; "maybe my knight is pinned, or maybe my knight is protecting something else"; "what's going to change if this piece goes on to join the attack? ... what obstacles is it going to face along its way? And what is my opponent going to do likely ... I'm going to spend as many milliseconds on this question as I estimate the worth of the stake ... every question should carry some sort of a bound or a probability distribution for a stake ... the worst case ... or the expected value should guide the decision, or our tolerance for risk")

WHAT THE CODE DID BEFORE THIS (78.41, read in the source): level 1 read reach from tables of the board as it stands (a blocker fixed, the other side never moving) and kept only the count of moves, the unit and the arrival place; the frame then played the FIRST move of a two-move way to an in-between place taken first in sorted order, found no new striker, and CLOSED the question as refuted; nothing was carried to the next position.

DESIGN
  LAYER ONE, THE MEDIUM  hops of a kind from place to place on the empty medium, from the movement rule alone (a concept file, the injected game layer; a table made once a game). A unit farther than the attack allows is closed with the count said.
  LAYER TWO, THE UNITS   for each geometric route, what stands against it as the board is. Not a list of shapes: AN OBSTACLE IS ANYTHING WHOSE ABSENCE WOULD LET THE STEP HAPPEN OR SUCCEED, found by asking the kernel the same question on the board without one unit, each unit in turn; and for a step that is legal but answered, the unit that made the answer, tested the same way; and time (the other side's faster way on as much). A finding read on a board without a unit is marked so.
  THE COST OF LEAVING    before a unit's route is read: what of its own side is newly lost once it has left its place (the cheap verdicts rerun after its first step). The route's worth is what it wins less the most it drops.
  THE ORDER PER UNIT     what changes if it leaves; what stands in its way; what the other side is likely to do. The third opens its own questions and is where the clock must be rationed.
  THE GRAPH              nodes are questions and claims with a verdict (confirmed, refuted, WAITING, not read); edges typed: needs, blocked_by, if_removed, holds, stopped_by, waits_on, breaks. A chain prints as "because ... ; if ... were gone then ...".
  WAITING ACROSS MOVES   October's waiting frame (what it waits on, what breaks it) kept from position to position with its read set; re-read only when a move touches the set.
  STAKES AS BOUNDS       every node holds a low and a high stake, tightened as answers come; and a CHANCE.
  THE CLOCK (next stage) the chance of a node from the measured base rates of its verdict kind in our own games (78.41 already printed them: lost where it stands 11 of 13 for theirs and 7 of 22 for mine; confirmed after an arrival 14 of 71 and 7 of 79; closed by reach 0 of 161), refit at sleep, no outside judge needed; a question's next step gets time in proportion to chance times stake over the cost of the step; for my own units the worst case (the high bound) leads, for theirs the expected value, the weight between the two a named parameter (the tolerance for risk). What the other side is likely to do is read from the same sheet from their side: their confirmed and waiting ways, by expected stake, are their likely moves, and those order the answers tried against my routes.
  REUSE                  October's frame search is in use; its fact store (read sets, stale flags) and waiting frames are to be used as they are where they fit, the game-bound parts behind the codec.
BEING BUILT (one builder, amendments in the order above): routes and whole-route following, the three verdicts, the pool, layers one and two, the removal test, the cost of leaving, the graph, bounds on nodes. Measures H (two-move ways, by verdict and by kind of route) and I (how many plies before a taking the unit was first under watch).

READ. The verdicts on my units did not move; one of theirs went from refuted to waiting. Moving aside explains few of the rejected removals: the steps with "no single unit" are mostly steps with two or more units in the way, which layer one already lists one by one as standing on a place passed over (see the printed chains: the corner unit's step along its own back row names three units and then says none). So the word "none" is wrong there: it is "several, each of which must go", and the follow-up should be asked of each in turn, cheapest first. The time per position fell, not to the earlier form's level. What remains is one thing: the goal sign after a leaving builds a whole reading of the child position. The narrow reading misses a small share of duties, all of the kind "goal unit newly under the sign", reported in the audit line.

STILL WRONG: (a2) the goal sign after a leaving needs to be computed from the changed places, not a whole reading; (c2) a step blocked by several units is called "none" and its follow-ups are not asked; (b), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h), (i) of the list above stand.

(c2): where no single removal frees a step and layer one names two or more units on it, the set is removed together (Params.joint, max_joint 3) and each member gets its follow-up, cheapest first, stopped at the first dead one. The chance: question_key (whose unit, verdict kind, moves the way needs, route group) with coarser prefixes as fallback; fit_chances counts, per key, whether the exact unit was taken within 4 and 8 plies in our own games (moves only; the judge's files are not opened, a test holds this); Chances smooths toward the next coarser key; Params.chances loads it and every question and node gets a chance. The clock: Params.clock present / chance / plain, Params.risk the dial (own units: risk times the upper bound plus the rest times the midpoint; the other side's: the midpoint), run with budget_seconds, budget_cost or max_steps. READ. (1) Several units together account for most of the former "none" steps; most such sets hold a member that cannot go, so the route stays refuted, now with the unit named. (2) The chance separates: "lost where it stands" and "live at level 0" are high, "waiting" sits at the base rate, "closed by no gain" is far under it; on unseen games the bands hold. (3) The clock by chance times stake is NOT better than the present order. With the dial at the worst case it spends its first steps on the asker's own units and reaches the other side's late; with the dial at the expected value most of that comes back, not all. The plain order, each question to its end in turn, is the worst under any small budget. Without a budget all three end alike, as they must. (4) The ceiling is the trouble, not the order: without a budget the sheet had raised danger on about one in five of my units that were then taken and about two in five of theirs; of the danger verdicts raised, about one in six of mine and two in five of theirs were followed by a taking. (5) Budgets under the cost of reading a position mean nothing: the reading and the goal unit's first step cost more than the budget.

STILL WRONG: the takings no danger verdict foresaw have not been looked at one by one (which kind they are decides what comes next); the reading of a position is the floor of the cost; the chance of a way node borrows the question's table; the other side's answers are not yet ranked by the same sheet from their side; (a2), (b), (d), (e), (g), (h), (i) stand.

NEXT: read the missed takings by kind (was the unit never flagged, flagged and refuted, or waiting) before more machinery; then the sheet on October's event kernel.

READ. Two things, and both are about the measure before they are about the reasoner. (1) "Taken" is not "lost". Of the other side's missed units most went in an exchange that was taken back at once: the sheet had read that exchange and called it worth nothing, and the game played it anyway; that verdict was right. Of my missed units most had MOVED before they were taken, many of them by taking something themselves, which the count calls a plain loss. (2) A question is asked about the place a unit stands on. A unit that walks to another place and is taken there is outside every question asked so far. That is the question of the move, not of the unit: "if this unit goes there, is it lost there", which the cornering frame already answers for one unit and nothing asks for the move about to be played.

NEXT, replacing the NEXT above: (i) measure J with LOSS in place of taking: the balance of worth over the exchange on that place, by the mined worths, so that an even exchange is not a miss and a unit that took more than it cost is not a loss; (ii) the question of the move: for the move about to be played (and the best few), the frame on the place it lands on and on what it leaves, which is the cost of leaving read for my own move; (iii) then the event kernel.


78.42 FOURTH FORM: LOSS IN PLACE OF TAKING; THE QUESTION OF THE MOVE (2026-11-13; question_sheet.py, the codec's `events`; tests 116). unit_loss: a unit is LOST when it is taken and the balance of worth over the run of takings on that place, its own arriving capture counted, is against its side; EVEN and GAINED otherwise. Measure J gained columns by LOSS; fit_chances takes outcome=loss (flag only, the table was not refitted). move_question(env, reading, move, params): (a) what the move leaves (cost_of_leaving, narrow), (b) where it lands (the exchange frame on the position after the move, what it took counted), (c) what the other side then has (units on changed places, the goal sign); verdict SAFE / LOSES / NOT SETTLED, explain_move, move_sheet over the legal moves under a budget; Params.move_question, off by default. READ. (1) With LOSS as the outcome the sheet foresees three in four of the other side's real losses; of my own, under one in three. The asymmetry is the finding: against their units the mover acts next, so what stands is what happens; against mine, the other side moves first and I move again before most losses land. (2) The question of the move is nearly always right when it says LOSES of the move played, and it says so rarely, because the search that played these games already avoids such moves. It calls about one legal move in five LOSES, and the move played is almost never one of them: as a screen it agrees with the search, it adds little to it on these games. (3) Of the 52 units that moved and were then taken, most were no loss at all by the balance; a few remain, and in the examples the loss came from a LATER own move or after the other side's next move, not from the move asked about. (4) Losses of my units within four plies are charged to the move played now, though a second own move lies in between: the measure must charge a loss to the last own move before it. (5) The cost of a move question is the reading of the position after the move; the frames cost nearly nothing.

STILL WRONG: K charges later moves' losses to this move; part (c) never fires because (a) reads the same units; units of the least worth are not asked about; the chance table is still fitted on taking; the reading of a position is the cost of everything (the kernel's facts call and the rows built from it).

NEXT: (i) K with each loss charged to the last own move before it; (ii) the mover's own losses need the other side's next move: the sheet asked from their side for their best open question, which is also "what is the opponent likely to do"; (iii) a cheaper reading of a child position (from the changed places, not anew); (iv) the event kernel.

Classes: A the unit already stood lost before the charged move (the sheet said so) and a move that kept it existed; B the charged move took the unit itself to where it was lost; C the charged move took away a guard or a shield; D neither: the other side's next move took another unit at once and this one went in the same exchange.

READ. At the move a loss is charged to, the sheet or the question of the move had SEEN the loss in most cases (A, B and C against D), and a move that the question of the move calls SAFE and that keeps the unit existed in nearly all. The games played the losing move anyway: they were played by the plain search, which never asked. So for losses of this kind the reasoner's sight is no longer the limit; what it sees is not yet USED. The unseen class D is small and mostly a second unit going in an exchange on a place the sheet had already marked. The count is small (one set of games), and this says nothing yet on what the SAFE moves cost elsewhere: the question of the move calls about one legal move in five LOSES, and a standing "lost" on my units is followed by a loss less than one time in three.

NEXT: USE. A player that takes the search's move, asks the sheet on standing losses and the question of the move on that move, and where the answer is LOSES or a standing loss is left without a keeper, asks the search's next choices in order until one is SAFE; played against the plain search at the same clock, measured by weighty units lost a game (unit_loss), by the result, and by 78.37's surprise rate. The reading of a position is the cost to cut for this.

    OBS (control) judge on overridden moves 0 (tolerance 0.02 expected result): override better 0, equal 0, worse 0; mean expected result played minus search's choice +nan, mean centipawns +nan

READ. (1) The guided player loses fewer weighty units than the plain search across the board from it, and the question of the move alone does most of that; the standing check alone does harm. (2) The result and the judge's mean loss barely move, and the judge calls the overrides about as often worse as better. (3) The guided player spends about four times the clock. The plain search GIVEN that same time beats the plain search by far more than the guided player does, on the result, on the balance of worth and on the judge's mean loss. So, as wired, the sheet is worth less than the time it costs: the same milliseconds are better spent searching. (4) The cost is the reading of positions in Python (the position, then the position after the move), not the frames. (5) Known wrong: a promotion is called a loss of the promoting unit; the next choices are not the search's own; games at the ply cap are left out of the scores.

NEXT: the sheet is not to stand beside the search as a veto in Python; what it knows has to cost near nothing and go INTO the search: (i) the reading of a child from the changed places and the sheet's cheap levels in Rust beside the kernel's facts, so that a move question costs what a frame costs; (ii) the verdicts as the search's ordering and as its quiet-move extension (a move the sheet calls LOSES searched last, a standing loss a reason to look one move deeper there), measured at EQUAL time against the plain search; (iii) fix promotion in unit_loss and the question of the move. The event kernel after that.

READ. (1) The cost is gone: the question of the move went from the cost of a whole search move to a small part of one, with the same verdicts except where the full form said NOT SETTLED for the goal sign. (2) At equal time the guided player does NOT beat the plain search: every guided score is under the control's, the judge calls the overrides worse about three times as often as better, and the guided player's lost units are a little under the control's, not clearly outside noise. (3) So the finding of the first form stands with the cost removed: replacing the search's move, on the word of a one-move reading of losses, by a move the search rated lower, does not help. What the sheet sees at one move the search at this clock mostly sees too, and where they differ the search is more often right.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE PLAN. The reasoner is not to second-guess the search on what the search can already see. Its use is where the search does not reach: the order in which things are looked at when the clock is short, and the things more than a few plies away (a way of two or three preparing moves, a waiting record that comes true). Both are 78.42's own subject (routes followed whole, waiting, the clock), and both were too slow to try in play before the light reading.

NEXT: (i) the whole sheet on the light reading (levels 0 to 2, the routes), with the audit against the full form, so that a position's sheet costs milliseconds; (ii) then the routes and the waiting records measured for what the search at its clock does NOT see: of the ways the sheet confirms at two or three moves, how many the search's own line at that clock contains or avoids; (iii) the sheet kept across the moves of a game on October's event kernel (what a move changes is re-asked, the rest served), which the light reading and the changed places make cheap; (iv) the goal sign in the light reading.

READ. (1) The light sheet gives the same verdict kinds as the full one on every question read, and the question of the move now agrees wholly since the goal sign is read. (2) A whole sheet is several times cheaper, not yet milliseconds: what remains is level 1's geometry in Python and the kernel's reason and census on the goal questions. (3) THE FINDING. Where no unit stands lost already, the ways of two or more moves the sheet confirms are few a game, the search at its clock already plays, answers or values most of them, and those it does not see come true about as often as not at all: the cell "the sheet confirms, the search does not see, the unit is lost" holds a handful of targets in all 16 games. The waiting records are many, the search sees almost none by these flags, and they come true at the base rate whether or not their condition came true. (4) In positions with the mover in check the sheet confirms many ways read from the board as it stands; they come true at the base rate: an artifact, in the full sheet too.

So on these games, at these clocks, the route reasoning does not see what the search misses often enough to count. The games are the search's own, which stops the comparison from being independent: a search that never walks into a prepared attack leaves none in its games to be found. The sheet's value against a stronger or a different opponent is unmeasured.

OPEN, for Kaveh: where the reasoner is to earn its place. The measured facts: it explains (chains with because and if-gone), it is right about standing losses, it agrees with the search at one move and adds nothing over it there, and its multi-move ways are rare and mostly seen by the search. Candidates not yet tried: the puzzle sets October was measured on (a prepared attack exists by construction, so the cell is not empty); games against a stronger opponent; the reasoner as the source of the search's ORDER inside the search rather than beside it.

STILL OWED: the sheet kept across the moves of a game on October's event kernel; a position in check read by the answers to the check, not as it stands.

READ. (1) CORRECT NOW. The first form served wrong verdicts because its read sets missed the units that bear on the route and the asker's context; with them, no served verdict differed from a fresh sheet on these games, nothing stale is served, waiting records wake on their condition and die by their break, and the store holds about a hundred live facts a game. (2) NO TIME SAVED. The kept sheet costs what a fresh one costs. Few verdicts survive a move untouched, and refuted ways are woken constantly; what a position costs is the reading of obstacles and reach, which is not what the memory holds. A recheck can almost never be settled cheaply. A cache of single frames would cost more in bookkeeping than it saves. (3) ONE AGENDA BY STAKE. At the two shortest budgets it holds a little more of the danger verdicts by stake than a fresh sheet, and fewer of them by count; from the middle budgets up it holds less, and its own bookkeeping runs over the budget. Kaveh's claim is not borne out as built: mostly refuted, by one run on a few games. (4) A waiting record woken by its condition is followed by a loss about three times as often as the base rate: the one new signal here; it has no cell in the fitted table yet. (5) October's Rust agenda is already game-free and could carry only the small Agenda class; the listeners, read sets and rechecks would stay where they are; the agenda is not where the time goes.

WHY THE MEMORY DOES NOT PAY, as far as these numbers show: the unit of memory is the verdict of a whole way, and a way reads many places, so most moves touch it. What would survive a move is smaller: the reach of one unit, the obstacle on one step, one exchange on one place. Those are what the time goes on, and they are not what is filed.

NEXT, not started: file the PARTS (a unit's reach, a step's obstacle, a place's exchange) with their own small read sets, so that a move wakes only the parts it touches and a way is re-put-together from parts still good; the agenda's bookkeeping inside the budget; the woken-waiting kind fitted into the chance table.

### 78.42: the event memory on by default (2026-11-14)

Kaveh's rule: cache when caching is not slower. The measure of the last section showed the same time kept as fresh and no wrong serve, so `run` and `read_position` now drain the pool's agenda by
default whenever a pool is carried (`refresh` defaults to `math.inf`; `refresh=None` is the old form, where a question asks for what a move touched). With no pool nothing changes, so the
match player, which carries none, plays as before. The one test of the old form is pinned to `refresh=None`. The four test files of the sheet: 212 passed.


### The high-level spec (2026-11-14)

Kaveh restated the target system: one graph of units, frames, facts and claims; tactical reasoning; frames from the bottom up; a policy toward tactical opportunity that talks in subgoals; sleep as an agent with tools whose step goal is to explain a surprise; Rust in the hot paths. It is written in docs/SYSTEM_SPEC.md. Every plan from here names the piece of that spec it serves.


## 78.43 THE QUESTION SHEET IN THE RUST ENGINE (Kaveh 2026-11-14: "go autonomous, while staying on path to the high level spec"; Rust first in the hot paths)

Serves docs/SYSTEM_SPEC.md sections 3 (tactical reasoning), 2 (the claims the graph waits for) and 8 (Rust in the hot paths).

WHY. A profile of the light sheet on 18 positions of the saved games (one run, directional): `OBS positions 18 seconds under profile 9.1`,
35957184 function calls. No single primitive holds the time: the route geometry (`geometric_routes`), the counterfactual obstacles, the board
edits of the codec and the interpreter's own calls share it; the one Rust call in it (`cs_engine.reason`) is about a ninth. So the speed is
not won by moving one function down; the sheet's core has to live in the engine, with the Python sheet kept as the readable mirror and as the
ORACLE the Rust form is checked against (the 72.7 precedent of Python twins).

WHAT, in stages, one commit each. No Cargo.toml is changed and no new crate is made: new modules go inside the existing layer crates (the
tactics crate), exposed through rust/engine/py/src/lib.rs. Never touched: rust/engine/gdl/src/lib.rs, rust/engine/game/src/gdl_game.rs,
rust/engine/Cargo.lock, any Cargo.toml. The layer modules name no object of any game (the source test of tests/test_plan78.py applies).

 A. THE READING AND THE ROUTES. The light reading in Rust (units with their places and worths, the strike and move tables, the distances
    between places, what bears on what as the board stands) and levels 0 and 1 by geometry (`level0`, `geometric_routes`, `_level1_geometry`
    and what they call). Whatever the Python codec supplies as the one game-specific place is supplied to the Rust form through one small
    trait or one data table, never by naming a game in the layer. ACCEPTANCE: on every position of the saved games where the Python light sheet
    reads, the Rust reading gives the same units, the same level 0 verdict per target and the same set of level 1 routes per target; every
    difference is listed with its position and cause. One timing line for each side.
 B. THE OBSTACLES AND THE FRAMES. Counterfactual removal (one unit, a goal unit moved aside, several jointly), the exchange and cornering frames
    (a Rust frame search equal to `frame_search.FrameSearch` on the frames the sheet builds), `settle_way`, the cost of leaving, the verdict of
    a way. ACCEPTANCE: the same verdict kind for every way of every target on the same positions.
 C. THE WHOLE SHEET AND THE MOVE QUESTION. The schedule (`run` with its clocks and budgets), `finish_levels`, `settle_flagged`, `unit_loss`,
    `move_question`. ACCEPTANCE: the same sheet (targets, verdict kinds, stakes) and the same move answers; the time per position printed.
 D. THE MEMORY. Read sets, listeners, waking and the drain in Rust, checked by the audit of 78.42 (served against fresh).

Then the uses that waited on speed: the opportunity number logged along every self-play game (SYSTEM_SPEC section 5), and the claims filed
as nodes of the engine's graph (section 2).

## 78.44 THE OPPORTUNITY NUMBER ALONG A GAME: is it a target worth steering by? (SYSTEM_SPEC section 5)

The policy of section 5 is to be trained toward "abundance of high-value tactical opportunity". Before any policy, the number itself is tested.
 - THE NUMBER. At a position, for the side to move: the sum over the other side's units of chance x worth for the open claims against them,
   minus the same sum for the claims against its own units. The chance is the fitted table's (data/derived/question_chances/fit1112.json, fitted
   on earlier games, so every game here is unseen by it); the claims are the Rust sheet's (`SheetModel.game`, clock present).
 - THE QUESTION. Does the number at a ply foretell the change of material over the next plies, beyond what the simplest count foretells?
   Outcome: the mover's balance of worth at 4, 8 and 16 plies ahead minus now. Baselines printed beside it: the same sum from the first level
   only (what can be taken at once), a count of claims with no chances, and the number with the positions shuffled within a game.
 - THE READING. A table by bands of the number (mean later change, count), and the rank correlation, for each horizon; by phase of the game;
   for the parts mine / theirs separately. On about 500 new self-play games of the control player. Nothing is fitted in this plan.
 - NEXT, only if the number foretells: log it for every legal move's child (which moves raise it), and fit the sparse subgoal statements.

DEFINITION AS BUILT. An open claim against a unit: the top verdict of its question is live0, live1, lost, confirmed, waiting or unsettled (closed1..3, refuted, idle0, idle1, unread are not open). Baselines: net0 = the same sum over the units level 0 read as live (chance of the table's cell (owner, live0)); count = open claims against theirs minus against mine; shuffled = net permuted among the plies of a game (seed fixed). READ (directional, one run on 500 games of one player). The number rises with the later change of material at all three horizons, and the shuffled control is near zero, so the rise is not an artefact of the ranking. It stands well above the plain count of claims (count: about 0.1). It does NOT stand much above the first-level baseline: net0 is within about 0.01 to 0.02 of net at each horizon, and the intervals of the two nearly overlap at 4 plies. Beyond the first level the reading is small: net - net0 has a correlation of about 0.2 and the partial rank correlation of net with net0 held out is about 0.19 / 0.18 / 0.15 at 4 / 8 / 16 plies; among the plies where net0 is zero (about 62 percent of them) net foretells almost nothing (about 0.05). The bands are not monotone: the mean outcome is about the same over the four lower bands and the whole rise is in the top band. net_d (danger kinds only) correlates better than net at every horizon, which says the waiting and level-1 claims add noise to the number as built. Gain predicts worth won and risk predicts worth lost, each about 0.3 to 0.4 at 4 plies; the correlation falls with the horizon. Caveats: the outcome is the material of the games of one player (a plain search at 0.2 s a move), including captures the first move of the horizon makes; a high net0 is probably often a capture on the board that the mover then makes (not separated here). Nothing here says the number steers a game.

Merged at 18acb02b. The number as the plan defined it is, on these games, mostly the first level: what can be taken at once. Beyond the first
level the builder's lines show a small remainder (the partial rank correlation and the plies where the first-level sum is zero), and the

has no target yet beyond one move. Two readings of why, not yet told apart: (1) the sheet's claims of more than one move are poor; (2) the
games are those of one searching player against itself, which parries what it sees, so a true prepared attack seldom comes true IN THESE GAMES
whatever its quality (SYSTEM_SPEC section 10: the chance depends on who answers). Plan 78.45 separates them where the answer is known by
construction; games against a weaker answerer are the other half and come after.

## 78.45 THE SHEET ON PUZZLES: does the route reasoning see a prepared attack that is there? (SYSTEM_SPEC section 3)

A puzzle is a position where a winning line of a few moves exists by construction. Sets: data/derived/ledger_puzzles_dev_300.json (to study
the misses) and ledger_puzzles_fresh_300.json (held out, read once at the end). Fields used: the position, the answer (first move), the
solution line, the themes, the rating. Measure only: nothing of the puzzles reaches the wake or any fit.
 - SEES: the sheet holds a claim for the side to move, in danger (lost or confirmed) against a unit of the other side or against their goal
   unit, whose way begins with the answer. PICKS: a plain chooser (the first move of the top such claim by stake) names the answer.
 - BASELINE beside it: the engine's plain search on the same position at the time the sheet took, and at 0.2 s.
 - THE MISSES, each put in one class by cause, by theme and by length of the solution: the target not on the sheet; the way not among the
   routes; the way read and refuted (with the stop that refuted it); not settled or not reached under the budget (the same sheet with a
   budget five times larger tells these apart); seen but outranked.
 - The four-way table: sheet sees / search finds.
The classes of misses are the work list for the reasoner; nothing is fixed in this plan.

### 78.45 READ BY THE PARENT (2026-11-15)

Merged at 0c60c7c2. On both sets the sheet holds a danger claim beginning with the answer in about four puzzles of ten and the plain search
names the answer in more than eight of ten at the same time; the sheet sees what the search misses in a handful only. So the first reading
of 78.44 holds: the sheet's claims of more than one move are the weak part, whoever answers. The misses by the builder's classes say what is
lacking. A way of the sheet is ONE unit travelling to strike ONE target. The answers it does not hold are moves that are not a step of such a
way: a move that makes a claim elsewhere and so forces the reply (a taking that removes a guard, a threat that draws a unit off, two claims
at once), and wins of the goal by a move outside the three scenarios kept. A way read alone is refuted by the target stepping aside (class
X) where the line works because the reply had to answer something else. The budget (class N) is the smaller part.

## 78.46 THE FORCING READ: a move, the claims it makes, every reply, the claims that stand (SYSTEM_SPEC section 3; Rust first, section 8)

Kaveh's design of 78.41 already names it: per move, what changes, and the opponent's reply; a double threat is a move whose claims no one
reply answers. October measured the same idea as lambda frames (catspace/incubator/analyst/lambda_frames.py); the literature calls it a
threat-space search. It is built in the Rust sheet first; the Python mirror is owed afterwards.
 - A THREAT MOVE of the side to move: a legal move after which, the board read as if that side moved again, a unit of the other side or
   their goal stands in danger that did not before, or a move that itself takes a unit.
 - THE READ. After a threat move EVERY legal reply is read (soundness: no reply is left out). For each reply: what the reply took, the claims
   of the move that still stand and what carrying out the best of them wins by the exchange on its place, and, where none stands, the mover's
   next threat moves, one level deeper, while the budget lasts. The goal is read by the engine's own forced-win clause (`force`). The value
   of the move is the least over the replies. A cut is NOT SETTLED, never a refutation and never a confirmation.
 - THE ANSWER, as claims: the move, the claims it makes, and for every reply which claim stands (the explanation of why the reply fails), the
   units won, the nodes read.
 - ACCEPTANCE. (1) Puzzles (78.45's measure, a second column): SEES and PICKS with the forcing read beside the sheet alone and the plain
   search, on dev_300 while building and fresh_300 once at the end; the misses left, by class. (2) SOUNDNESS, on ordinary positions of the
   held games: every claim the forcing read confirms is checked against the engine's ledger search at a depth that covers the line; the
   share it contradicts is printed, and each contradiction is read. A confirmation the search contradicts is a bug or a named limit, never
   a tolerated rate. (3) The sheet's existing answers do not change: the 78.43 measures still print zero differences.
